Introduction The revised Bloom’s Taxonomy of Learning suggests that higher learning, involving procedural and metacognitive knowledge, is engaged when students can interact with learning processes. This includes carrying out a procedure (apply), detecting how parts of a process or theory relate to one another (analyze), making judgements based on criteria (evaluate), and designing an original product (create) [1]. In order to engage with these higher levels of learning, classroom structures must move beyond classical lecturing (passive learning) to provide students with organized experiences in which they can interact with course content more directly (active learning). The Learning Pyramid provides a simplified view of the success of learning strategies on knowledge retention, showcasing that active learning techniques, flipped classrooms (teaching), or laboratories (practice) lead to better knowledge retention (Figure 1). While the percentages of knowledge retention reported within the Learning Pyramid are debated [2], the framework highlights that active learning strategies are in line with achieving higher learning, as described by Bloom. In general, active learning techniques can be categorized into four themes: (1) individual nonpolling (e.g., concept maps); (2) in-class polling (e.g., iClickers or TopHat); (3) whole-class discussions (e.g., case studies or worked problems); and (4) collaborative team-based activities (e.g., worksheets, games, or hands-on activities) [3]. In all cases, the goals within a learning experience are centralized on providing students with new knowledge, creating opportunities for skill development, challenging preconceived notions, and developing beneficial behaviors. Active learning in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) classrooms is a well-established, and now commonly used, practice to increase student performance [4,5,6,7,8]. For example, research by Freeman et al. showcases that active learning can increase the average student examination performance by a half a letter grade while, similarly, lowering the failure rate by 55%, compared to lecture-only courses [4]. In first-year general chemistry, Mutambuki et al. have shown that a combination of metacognition (ability to plan, monitor, and evaluate one’s own understanding and performance [9]) and active learning significantly increases students’ exam performance, lowers the number of “D” and “F” letter grades, and lowers the number of course withdrawals [10]. Similar work has shown that active learning in other undergraduate chemistry courses significantly improves student outcomes, most noted in students with lower academic achievement levels [11] and underrepresented groups [12]. Despite the benefits of active learning, student perceptions of active learning techniques as efficient tools for teaching can be mixed depending on the technique chosen [7,13,14,15]. For example, in-person discussion-based activities or team-based activities are often well received by chemistry students [16] compared to online discussion forums where student engagement can be low [17,18,19]. The benefits of active learning highlight the need to develop thoughtful engagement opportunities in which students can explore learning together through guided discussion-based activities [14,15]. The application of gamified learning materials is an excellent method to engage students, incorporating opportunities for hands-on application of learning objectives, allowing for multimodal learning and team communication. The benefits of gamified learning and the application of escape rooms as immersive learning experience are outlined herein. The unique design of escape rooms not only allows for discussion-focused engagement but provides an avenue for students to apply key learning objectives in a “real-world” experience. In this review, we present an overview of the current literature around the use of escape-room-style puzzles in chemical education and provide practical guides for instructors looking to incorporate these tools. Additionally, we provide context about the pedagogical value of escape-room-style puzzles, a summary of assessment methods which can be used for active learning techniques (such as this one), and a future outlook on using these tools. 1.1. This learning cycle is often reflected in experimental development in which learners draw on knowledge gained in previous experiences to develop or improve new processes and gameplay, taking place multiple times as the game proceeds [22]. Gamification of learning is defined as the application of gaming components into non-gaming environments. The desire to improve problem solving and increase student motivation [23], has grown in popularity in recent years [24]. fetched_contents.text: Periodical | Using Escape Rooms in the Chemistry Classroom Figure 1. A key is an essential component of the escape room activities. An escape room is defined in the Cambridge English Dictionary as, “a game where people are locked into a room and have to find a way to escape by finding clues.” In the chemistry classroom, instead of being simply a game, the escape room idea can be used to help students learn chemical concepts. It has been shown that active learning increases students’ interest in what they are studying.1 As science teachers, we have many ways to get students out of their seats to manipulate chemicals and equipment. Traditional laboratory experiments are one way in which we accomplish this, but the “cookbook” nature of those experiments often leads to students’ lack of interest and short attention spans. By reimagining these experiments through the lens of escape rooms, I have devised activities designed to increase student interest and focus. In this article, I’ll describe two very different escape rooms that I have successfully used with my classes. Both of the activities are available in the AACT Classroom Resource Library. Advantages of using escape rooms One aspect of using escape rooms in the classroom is giving the students the experience of working in groups. Learning how to work in groups has become a very valuable skill in the workplace, yet students in the classroom often resist group work or do not use it effectively.2 In the activities described below, cooperation among the group members is emphasized. The students are grouped by ability, so that no single group member is carrying the group while the others merely observe. Students are carefully observed by the teacher during the activity for their interaction and social dynamics, and part of their grade is based on those observations. Another important aspect of the escape room is getting buy-in from the students. The escape room adds a competitive element that increases students’ motivation to work together to achieve their goals. The students are engaged by the activity, and their desire to participate is increased. Students have to literally find locks and keys in order to “escape.” Each part of the escape room involves a laboratory activity that the students already have some familiarity with. They then need to apply that knowledge to the new situation to be successful. Escape rooms allow for differentiation of the lesson. By making clues to the solution available to the students, the lesson can be scaffolded as needed. In my classroom, I’ve accomplished this in two ways. One way was to have the same clues available for each group — but the students had to choose whether or not to buy the clues (the “price” was a 10-point deduction from their grade). The other way was for me to provide clues from the start, but with the clues differentiated based on the ability of the members of the group. Activity 1: The Thermodynamics Escape Room for AP Chemistry The first escape room activity I developed was for my Advanced Placement Chemistry class, because I was looking for a way to vary the activities in the classroom. My school’s periods are 80-minute blocks, and keeping students engaged for that long can be challenging. Escape rooms are very popular in our local area, and I assumed my students had heard of them — if not actually participated in them. I have never participated in a commercial escape room myself, but I do know that it is a very immersive activity. There is a scenario to follow, clues to find and unravel, and an actual room to escape from. I wanted the escape room that I developed to have those same characteristics. I spent a long time at the hardware store, looking at keys and locks, and even more time at home, playing with possibilities and deciding what would and wouldn’t work. It was very important to me to have actual keys and actual locks — and every escape room I’ve written uses those components. For my first escape room, I decided to have the activity function as an assessment. In AP Chemistry, I find that students often do not manage to show what they know on a test. Sometimes this is because they are nervous; other times, it is because they feel rushed, and as a result they rely on memory rather than thinking the problem through. I felt that by doing a nontraditional assessment, I would gain a better understanding of what my students understood about a very challenging chemistry topic. I also felt that students had to work in groups for this assignment. Not only would this save on resources, but more importantly, it would force students to think through the problem. By having the students do group work, I could listen to the students talk with each other, and thus have another metric with which to assess them. I made sure, however, to assign the groups for this activity, and did let the students choose their own partners. I wanted to group them by ability, because I wanted everyone to participate equally. I also did not want one person making the decisions and the other people in the group simply agreeing. To ensure equal participation, I included in my rubric that the proctor would be observing group dynamics and could deduct or add points for any individual in the group based on their participation. This ended up working very well. I knew the relative abilities of the students in the class, so I grouped them by level, and it was very clear which groups figured out the tasks quickly, and which were struggling. To make sure the tasks could be completed in the time allotted, I built in clues that students could “buy” if they were stuck. I had three clues ready (one for each task). I did not want the students to give up immediately and go straight for the clues, so I added a time of 10 minutes before they could even ask for the clue. Hands-on activities in chemistry escape rooms are designed to make learning tangible by requiring players to perform physical actions, apply chemistry knowledge, and use lab tools. The evidence consistently points to a mix of “wet” and “dry” puzzle types: “wet” puzzles require hands-on lab activity with equipment and chemicals, while “dry” puzzles rely more on thinking without hands-on work [N1-R2]. This distinction helps explain how players progress: they may physically manipulate equipment, mix substances, or observe reactions, and then use the results to unlock locks [N1-R2].

The physical actions players perform to progress are varied but generally include manipulating equipment, reading measurements, and solving lab-based tasks. One example is a chemistry escape room where students solve interactive science challenges focused on the properties of matter, states of matter, mixtures, and other physical chemistry topics, with the goal of opening a lock [N4-R4]. Another example is a digital escape room where students are assigned numbers after solving puzzles, and those numbers are combined into a four-digit code to open a lock [N4-R3]. The review article also notes that escape-room-style puzzles can include immersive, paper-based, Battle Boxes, condensed escape activities, and online/virtual formats, indicating a spectrum of physical interaction levels [N1-R1]. A concrete classroom example describes students working in groups to solve laboratory activities and apply that knowledge to escape the room, with actual keys and locks used throughout [N3-F2].

Chemistry knowledge is required to unlock locks by linking puzzle solutions to specific concepts. The evidence shows that locks are often tied to chemistry topics such as chemical reactions, equations, stoichiometry, and periodic properties, so players must use these concepts to find clues and generate correct codes [N3-F2][N3-R2][N5-R5]. In one classroom activity, the chemical reaction 2Al(s) + 3CuCl₂(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3Cu(s) is used, and students wear goggles as part of the lab procedure [N2-R5]. Another example is a digital escape room where a conductivity table is filled out, and the resulting numbers form a code for a lock [N6-R4]. This shows that chemistry knowledge is not only about memorizing facts, but also about interpreting experimental results and applying them to a lock mechanism [N6-R4].

Common tools or materials used in the activities include locks, keys, combination locks, chemicals, equipment, and sometimes specialized lab apparatus. The review article explicitly mentions that escape rooms can use actual keys and actual locks, and that each escape room described uses those components [N3-F2]. The classroom example also notes that students use goggles, and the laboratory escape room paper describes “wet chemistry manipulations unique to the chemistry laboratory” [N3-F2][N3-R5]. Other evidence points to a combination lock requiring a three-digit code obtained by balancing chemical calculations [N2-R2], as well as physical tasks such as placing hands in a circuit to complete a lock mechanism [N2-R1]. Overall, the tools and materials are chosen to reinforce lab skills while keeping the lock mechanism tied to chemistry content [N1-R2][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## Chemistry escape rooms: how hands-on activities unlock locks and what puzzles they typically include

Chemistry escape rooms combine active learning with game mechanics to make science engaging and memorable. The core idea is that players must solve chemistry-based puzzles to unlock locks, with the hands-on activities designed to make the learning experience concrete and immersive. Across the branch reports, the pattern is clear: chemistry escape rooms use physical actions, lab tools, and chemistry knowledge to progress, while the puzzles span chemical reactions, lab procedures, and logical tasks [N1-R2][N2-R5][N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-R4][N6-R4].

---

## 1. How hands-on activities are used to unlock locks

### Physical actions players perform to progress
Players in chemistry escape rooms often perform physical actions such as manipulating equipment, mixing chemicals, reading measurements, and solving lab-based tasks. The evidence distinguishes “wet” puzzles, which require hands-on lab activity with equipment and chemicals, from “dry” puzzles that rely more on thinking without hands-on work [N1-R2]. This means that the escape room is not just about answering questions—it often involves a real lab-like experience.

In practice, players may:

- Work in groups to solve laboratory activities [N3-F2]
- Manipulate combination locks, keys, or other physical mechanisms [N3-F2]
- Read tables, conduct measurements, and interpret data [N6-R4]
- Use lab equipment and chemicals to observe reactions and generate clues [N3-R5][N2-R5]

These physical actions are designed to reinforce lab skills and make chemistry feel like a real process rather than a set of abstract formulas.

### How chemistry knowledge is required to unlock locks
Chemistry knowledge is central to unlocking locks. The escape room is not a generic puzzle game; it is tied to specific chemistry concepts. The branch reports show that puzzles are linked to topics such as chemical reactions, equations, stoichiometry, hydrates, percent composition, Lewis dot structures, chemical bonding, and redox chemistry [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5][N4-F3]. Players must therefore use their understanding of these topics to find clues and generate the correct code.

For example:

- One classroom escape room uses the chemical reaction 2Al(s) + 3CuCl₂(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3Cu(s) [N2-R5]
- A digital escape room uses a conductivity table to derive a numerical code for a lock [N6-R4]
- A ChemEscape activity focuses on redox chemistry, thermodynamics, and chemical equilibria [N3-R1]

In these cases, the lock is not opened by luck or guesswork. It is opened by applying chemistry knowledge to a puzzle, which makes the escape room both challenging and educational [N2-R2][N6-R4].

### Common tools or materials used in the activities
The branch reports highlight a range of tools and materials that make chemistry escape rooms tangible:

- **Locks and keys**: Many escape rooms use actual keys and actual locks [N3-F2]
- **Combination locks**: Some puzzles require a three-digit code obtained from balancing chemical calculations [N2-R2]
- **Lab equipment and chemicals**: “Wet” puzzles involve hands-on lab activity with equipment and chemicals [N1-R2][N3-R5]
- **Tables and data sheets**: Conductivity tables, measurement tables, and other data sheets are used to generate codes [N6-R4]
- **Digital tools**: Online and digital escape rooms use platforms like Google Forms and other interactive systems [N4-F3]

These materials help create a realistic, immersive experience where the lock mechanism is tied to the science itself [N3-F2][N4-F3].

---

## 2. What types of chemistry puzzles are typically included

Chemistry escape rooms typically include a mix of puzzle types, with the evidence pointing to three main categories: puzzles based on chemical reactions or equations, puzzles involving measurement or lab procedures, and puzzles that require pattern recognition or logic.

### Puzzles based on chemical reactions or equations
This is one of the most common puzzle types. The branch reports show that escape rooms often use reaction-based tasks, such as:

- Balancing chemical equations [N3-R2]
- Identifying reaction products and types [N3-R2]
- Using reaction stoichiometry and chemical bonding concepts [N4-F3][N3-R2]
- Redox chemistry tasks [N3-R1]

A concrete example is the reaction 2Al(s) + 3CuCl₂(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3Cu(s), used in a classroom escape room [N2-R5]. Another example is a ChemEscape activity that includes redox and thermodynamics puzzles [N3-R1]. These puzzles train students to apply reaction-based knowledge rather than just memorize facts.

### Puzzles involving measurement or lab procedures
Measurement and lab procedure puzzles are also common, especially in “wet” escape rooms. The evidence shows that these puzzles often involve:

- Reading measurements and interpreting tables [N6-R4]
- Performing lab tasks such as mixing, observing reactions, and recording results [N3-F2][N3-R5]
- Using equipment and chemicals in a lab-like setting [N1-R2]

The review article explicitly contrasts “wet” puzzles with “dry” puzzles, showing that hands-on measurement and lab work are a major part of the escape-room experience [N1-R2]. The classroom example also shows students solving laboratory activities and using that knowledge to escape the room [N3-F2].

### Puzzles that require pattern recognition or logic
Escape rooms also include logic-based and pattern-based puzzles. The branch reports indicate that these puzzles may not always be purely chemical, but they still reinforce scientific thinking.

- The review article describes escape rooms as including immersive, paper-based, Battle Boxes, condensed escape activities, and online/virtual formats [N1-R1]
- The classroom example emphasizes group problem-solving and scaffolded clues, implying logical deduction is part of the process [N3-F2]
- The digital escape room example uses a conductivity table and a numerical code derived from that table, which requires pattern recognition [N6-R4]

These logic-based puzzles help students develop higher-order thinking skills such as analysis, inference, and code-breaking [N1-R1][N6-R4].

---

## 3. How lock mechanisms and verification systems work

In chemistry escape rooms, the lock mechanism is designed so that correct chemistry answers trigger the lock, combination codes are generated from puzzle solutions, and answers are verified by the lock itself rather than by an external judge.

### Locks triggered by correct chemistry answers
The evidence shows that the lock is tied directly to the solution of a chemistry problem. A classroom escape room uses a combination lock requiring a three-digit code obtained by balancing one of the puzzles [N2-R2]. Another example uses a conductivity table and derives a numerical code for a corresponding lock [N6-R4]. The classroom example also describes students solving laboratory activities and using actual keys and locks to escape [N3-F2].

This means the lock is not just a symbolic “door.” It is a real mechanism that only opens when the players’ chemistry reasoning is correct [N2-R2][N3-F2][N6-R4].

### How combination codes are generated from puzzles
Combination codes are often generated from puzzle solutions through numerical interpretation or pattern recognition. One classroom escape room assigns students numbers after solving their puzzle, and those numbers are combined into a four-digit code to open a lock [N4-R3]. The digital escape room example uses a conductivity table and a numerical code derived from it [N6-R4]. The review article also mentions a conductivity table and complex locking mechanisms, showing that the code may come from a measurement table rather than a single equation [N6-R4].

In other words, the code is not arbitrary. It is generated by transforming the puzzle’s solution into a numerical or symbolic form [N4-R3][N6-R4].

Answers are verified through the lock mechanism itself. The evidence points to two main ways:

This design makes the escape room more immersive and immediate: the lock is both the goal and the proof of successful problem solving [N2-R2][N3-F2][N6-R4].

One classroom escape room is explicitly framed as a nontraditional assessment in which students apply knowledge to escape the room [N3-F2]. The review article also emphasizes that escape-room-style puzzles can be used to reinforce concepts in chemical bonding [N4-F3].

This means the clues are not just random hints; they are conceptually grounded and intended to deepen understanding [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### Time pressure and teamwork affect the experience
Time pressure and teamwork are important design elements. The classroom example notes that escape rooms add a competitive element that increases motivation and requires students to work together to achieve goals [N3-F2]. ## 3. How lock mechanisms and verification systems work

In chemistry escape rooms, the lock mechanism is designed so that correct chemistry answers trigger the lock, combination codes are generated from puzzle solutions, and answers are verified by the lock itself rather than by an external judge.

### Locks triggered by correct chemistry answers
The evidence shows that the lock is tied directly to the solution of a chemistry problem. A classroom escape room uses a combination lock requiring a three-digit code obtained by balancing one of the puzzles [N2-R2]. Another example uses a conductivity table and derives a numerical code for a corresponding lock [N6-R4]. The classroom example also describes students solving laboratory activities and using actual keys and locks to escape [N3-F2].

This means the lock is not just a symbolic “door.” It is a real mechanism that only opens when the players’ chemistry reasoning is correct [N2-R2][N3-F2][N6-R4].

### How combination codes are generated from puzzles
Combination codes are often generated from puzzle solutions through numerical interpretation or pattern recognition. One classroom escape room assigns students numbers after solving their puzzle, and those numbers are combined into a four-digit code to open a lock [N4-R3]. The digital escape room example uses a conductivity table and a numerical code derived from it [N6-R4]. The review article also mentions a conductivity table and complex locking mechanisms, showing that the code may come from a measurement table rather than a single equation [N6-R4].

In other words, the code is not arbitrary. It is generated by transforming the puzzle’s solution into a numerical or symbolic form [N4-R3][N6-R4].

### How answers are verified or locked
Answers are verified through the lock mechanism itself. The evidence points to two main ways:

1. The lock accepts a code only when the players’ answer is correct [N2-R2]
2. The lock is triggered by a specific chemical result or measurement outcome [N6-R4]

The classroom example explicitly describes students working in groups and using actual keys and locks, suggesting that the lock is a physical verification system rather than a separate check by the instructor [N3-F2]. The digital escape room example further shows that a filled-out table can be used to derive a code for the lock, making the verification process immediate and integrated into the game [N6-R4].

This design makes the escape room more immersive and immediate: the lock is both the goal and the proof of successful problem solving [N2-R2][N3-F2][N6-R4].

## 4. How escape-room design balances difficulty and educational value

Escape-room design in chemistry classrooms is intended to balance challenge with learning. The branch reports show that clues are structured to teach chemistry concepts, time pressure and teamwork shape the experience, and the lock mechanism itself reinforces learning.

### Clues are structured to teach chemistry concepts
The evidence shows that escape rooms are designed around specific chemistry topics, such as chemical reactions, equations, stoichiometry, hydrates, percent composition, Lewis dot structures, chemical bonding, and redox chemistry [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5][N4-F3]. One classroom escape room is explicitly framed as a nontraditional assessment in which students apply knowledge to escape the room [N3-F2]. The review article also emphasizes that escape-room-style puzzles can be used to reinforce concepts in chemical bonding [N4-F3].

This means the clues are not just random hints; they are conceptually grounded and intended to deepen understanding [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### Time pressure and teamwork affect the experience
Time pressure and teamwork are important design elements. The classroom example notes that escape rooms add a competitive element that increases motivation and requires students to work together to achieve goals [N3-F2]. It also explains that students are grouped by ability to ensure equal participation, and that group dynamics are part of the grade [N3-F2]. Time pressure is further implied by the use of a limited time window before students can access clues and by the need to complete tasks within an 80-minute class period [N3-F2].

This design makes the experience more intense and interactive, pushing students to think quickly and communicate effectively [N3-F2].

### Answers are verified or locked in a learning-friendly way
Answers are verified through the lock mechanism itself, which means students receive immediate feedback. The evidence shows that correct chemistry answers trigger locks, and combination codes are generated from puzzle solutions [N2-R2][N4-R3][N6-R4]. The classroom example also describes a system where students can buy clues, but only after a 10-minute delay, which scaffolds difficulty and prevents immediate reliance on hints [N3-F2].

This means the escape room is not just a game; it is a learning tool that reinforces chemistry knowledge through trial, error, and verification [N3-F2][N4-R3][N6-R4].

## Conclusion

Chemistry escape rooms incorporate hands-on activities by requiring players to perform physical actions, apply chemistry knowledge, and use lab tools such as locks, keys, combination locks, chemicals, and measurement tables [N1-R2][N3-F2][N3-R5][N6-R4]. The puzzles typically include chemical reactions and equations, measurement or lab procedures, and logic-based tasks [N2-R5][N3-R1][N3-R2][N6-R4]. Lock mechanisms are triggered by correct chemistry answers, and combination codes are generated from puzzle solutions, with answers verified by the lock itself [N2-R2][N4-R3][N6-R4].
